summary_zh: 學會在客戶抱怨時先傾聽、再說明規定與下一步，並用 have to／be supposed to／had better 講清楚「必須、照規定應該、最好」。

replies.zh: 今天翻譯第 2、3 題直接練 had already sent（過去完成式：在那之前已經做完）和 had been tracking（過去完成進行式：到那時為止一直在做）；複習題也再練一次 have grown／has canceled。

vocab.definition: a period when a system or service is not working
vocab.example: The four-hour outage stopped every customer from logging in.
vocab.example_zh: 這次四小時的服務中斷讓所有客戶都無法登入。

vocab.definition: to pass a problem to someone more senior so they can deal with it
vocab.example: If the bug isn't fixed in two hours, escalate it to the engineering lead.
vocab.example_zh: 如果兩小時內沒修好這個 bug，就往上呈報給工程主管。

vocab.definition: to express strong feelings, especially anger, so that you feel better
vocab.example: Let the customer vent for a minute before you explain anything.
vocab.example_zh: 在你解釋任何事之前，先讓客戶發洩一下。

vocab.definition: a temporary way of getting something done while the real problem is not fixed
vocab.example: Until the fix is ready, the workaround is to export the data by hand.
vocab.example_zh: 在修好之前，暫時的替代做法是手動匯出資料。

vocab.definition: to find out the real cause of a problem
vocab.example: Our engineers are working to get to the bottom of the crash.
vocab.example_zh: 我們的工程師正在查當機的真正原因。

vocab.definition: to be forgotten or not dealt with because nobody is clearly responsible
vocab.example: Requests like this can fall through the cracks if nobody owns them.
vocab.example_zh: 如果沒人負責，這類請求很容易被忽略。

vocab.definition: to allow something that is not usually allowed because of special circumstances
vocab.example: We don't usually give refunds, but my manager agreed to bend the rules this time.
vocab.example_zh: 我們通常不退款，但這次主管同意通融。

vocab.zh: 表達善意的舉動（如補償、優惠）
vocab.definition: something you give or do to show that you want to keep a good relationship
vocab.example: As a goodwill gesture, we gave the client a month of free service.
vocab.example_zh: 為了表達誠意，我們送客戶一個月的免費服務。

reading.title: The Client Who Almost Left
paragraphs: Last Thursday, our biggest logistics client, Northway, was hit by a four-hour outage in the middle of their busiest week. By the time I got to my desk, their operations director, Dana, had already sent three emails, each one angrier than the last. The problem wasn't new, either. A similar issue had flared up in September, and our fix clearly hadn't held.

My manager, Priya, gave me some advice before I called: "Let her vent first. You don't have to defend the product, and you'd better not promise anything you can't deliver." Under our policy, we're supposed to escalate any outage longer than two hours to the engineering lead, so I messaged him before I dialed.

Dana was frustrated, and with good reason. Her team had been tracking shipments by hand all morning, and two of her drivers had missed pickups. In September, she said, her request had fallen through the cracks because nobody followed up after the first fix. I listened, apologized without making excuses, and told her that our engineers were working to get to the bottom of it. In the meantime, I walked her team through a workaround that let them export shipment data every hour.

Dana's contract only covers outages longer than six hours, so technically we didn't have to offer anything. Priya decided to bend the rules a little. As a goodwill gesture, we gave Northway a month of free service, and any unused support hours will carry over to next year. We also promised a weekly update until the root cause is fixed.
Yesterday, Dana sent a short email: "Thanks for not hiding from this." It was the friendliest message she had sent us all year.

questions.q: Why was Dana especially angry about this outage?
options: It was the first problem Northway had ever had.
A similar problem had happened in September.
Her contract had just ended.
Priya had refused to call her.
questions.explain_zh: 第 1 段：「A similar issue had flared up in September, and our fix clearly hadn't held.」同樣的問題九月就發生過，修好又壞。

questions.q: What did the writer do while the engineers looked for the cause?
options: Gave Dana a full refund
Showed Dana's team a temporary way to export data
Visited Northway's drivers
Asked Dana to call the engineering lead
questions.explain_zh: 第 3 段：「I walked her team through a workaround that let them export shipment data every hour.」

questions.q: What does Dana's last email suggest?
options: She is still planning to cancel the contract.
She appreciated that the company dealt with the problem openly.
She wants another month of free service.
She didn't read the weekly updates.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。「Thanks for not hiding from this」是感謝他們沒有逃避、坦白處理，而且作者說這是她整年最友善的一封信。

grammar.point: Modals of obligation and advice: have to, be supposed to, had better
grammar.point_zh: 表示義務與建議：have to、be supposed to、had better

guide.key_zh: 非做不可用 have to；照規定或安排應該用 be supposed to；不做會出事用 had better

uses.note_zh: don't have to = 不必，不是「不可以」

uses.form: S + be + supposed to + V（原形）
uses.signal: under our policy, by Friday, but…
uses.note_zh: 過去式 was/were supposed to 常表示「本來應該，結果沒做到」
口語縮寫 you'd better，後面不加 to；雖然有 had，但講的是現在或未來；語氣像警告

mistakes.wrong: You had better to call her now.
mistakes.why_zh: had better 後面直接接原形動詞，不加 to

mistakes.wrong: The support lead have to reply within two hours.
mistakes.right: The support lead has to reply within two hours.
mistakes.why_zh: 主詞是單數（the support lead），要用 has to

mistakes.wrong: You don't have to share client data. It's against the rules.
mistakes.right: You can't share client data. It's against the rules.
mistakes.why_zh: 「不可以」要用 can't／mustn't；don't have to 是「不必」

examples.en: A manager has to approve every refund.
examples.zh: 每一筆退款都要經過主管核准。

examples.en: You don't have to stay late. The fix can wait until tomorrow.
examples.zh: 你不必留下來加班，修正可以等到明天。

examples.en: We were supposed to update the client on Monday, but nobody did.
examples.zh: 我們本來應該星期一跟客戶更新進度，結果沒人做。

examples.en: You'd better call Dana before she escalates it to your boss.
examples.zh: 你最好在 Dana 把事情鬧到你老闆那裡之前先打給她。

exercises.q: Under our policy, every new hire ___ (have to) finish security training in the first week.
exercises.explain_zh: 題目指定用 have to：規定要求、一定得做 → have to。主詞 every new hire 是單數，要用 has to。（也可以說 is supposed to，但語氣較弱，常暗示「規定是這樣，實際不一定做到」。）

exercises.q: You look exhausted. You'd better ___ (go) home and rest.
exercises.explain_zh: had better（'d better）後面直接接原形動詞，不加 to：You'd better go。

exercises.q: The update ___ (be supposed to) go out yesterday, but it was delayed.
exercises.explain_zh: yesterday 是過去，而且「本來應該、結果沒做到」→ was supposed to。主詞 the update 是單數，用 was。

exercises.q: It's only a small bug, so the customer ___ (not / have to) reinstall the app.
exercises.explain_zh: 「不必」→ don't have to。主詞 the customer 是單數，要用 doesn't have to（不是 don't）。

exercises.q: Under the contract, we ___ reply within 24 hours, but we took three days.
options: were supposed to
had better
don't have to
are going to
exercises.explain_zh: 合約規定要 24 小時內回覆，但實際花了三天 → 「本來應該、結果沒做到」用 were supposed to。後半句 but we took three days 是關鍵線索。

options: You'd better test it before the demo, or it might crash.
You don't have to test it before the demo.
You were supposed to test it yesterday.
You've tested it twice already.
exercises.explain_zh: had better 表示「最好…，不然會出事」，後面的 or it might crash 就是警告的後果。其他三句分別是「不必」、「本來應該」、「已經做過」。

review.point_zh: 現在完成式 vs 過去簡單式

exercises.q: Since the new version launched, sign-ups ___ (grow) by 18%.
exercises.explain_zh: since 到現在、而且有具體數字（18%）→ 用 have + p.p.（have grown），不用進行式 have been growing。

exercises.q: The client ___ (cancel) three orders so far this month.
exercises.explain_zh: so far this month（到目前為止）＋次數（three orders）→ 現在完成式。主詞 the client 是單數，要用 has。

options: did you notice
have you noticed
have you been noticed
are you noticing
exercises.explain_zh: When 問的是過去某個明確時間點 → 用過去式 did you notice，不用現在完成式；have you been noticed 是被動，意思也不對。

guide.key_zh: 先問自己：句子裡有沒有說「何時」？有明確的過去時間就用過去式；沒說何時、或一路延續到現在，就用完成式

uses.label_zh: 過去某個時間點發生、已經結束
uses.signal: last night, at 6 a.m., two months ago, in May
uses.note_zh: 能回答 When? 的句子，幾乎都用過去式

uses.label_zh: 沒說何時，重點是「現在的結果」或「經驗」
uses.note_zh: 美式口語常把 just、already、yet 和過去式連用（I just got my boarding pass.），也是正確的；考試與正式寫作建議用完成式。

uses.label_zh: 從過去一直延續到現在
uses.signal: since then, for three years, so far
uses.note_zh: 中文說「我在這裡從半夜到現在」，英文不能用現在式 I am here since…

mistakes.wrong: I have missed my flight last night.
mistakes.right: I missed my flight last night.
mistakes.why_zh: 有 last night 這種明確的過去時間，只能用過去式

mistakes.wrong: I am at this airport since midnight.
mistakes.right: I have been at this airport since midnight.
mistakes.why_zh: since 表示「到現在」，要用完成式，不能用現在式

mistakes.wrong: Ticket prices have been gone up since May.
mistakes.right: Ticket prices have gone up since May.
mistakes.why_zh: go 是不及物動詞，沒有被動；have been gone 只用在「離開多久了」（He's been gone for an hour）。「價格上漲」只要 have gone up

timeline.label: My flight left Taipei three hours late last night.
I've just gotten my new boarding pass.
I've been at this airport since midnight.

listening.title: Invoices That Didn't Go Out

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Laura
lines.text: Tom, I'm on a layover in Dubai, and I've just found out our invoices didn't go out this morning. What happened?

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Tom
lines.text: I'm really sorry, Laura. There was a short outage overnight, and the scheduled jobs didn't run. I've already escalated it to our engineers.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Laura
lines.text: This is the second time this month. My finance team has to get those invoices out by Friday, or we won't get paid until next month.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Tom
lines.text: I understand. You don't have to wait for the fix, though. There's a workaround: your team can send them manually from the billing page.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Laura
lines.text: Manually? We're supposed to be saving time with your software, not adding work.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Tom
lines.text: You're right, and that's not good enough. If it helps, someone on my team can send them for you within the hour.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Laura
lines.text: Okay, that would help. But you'd better make sure nothing falls through the cracks this time.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Tom
lines.text: I'll check every invoice myself and send you a list before your connecting flight.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Laura
lines.text: My flight boards at four, Dubai time. And I want to know what actually caused this.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Tom
lines.text: Of course. We're going to get to the bottom of it, and you'll have a written report by Wednesday.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Laura
lines.text: Thanks, Tom. Sorry for snapping at you. It's been a long trip, and I'm feeling a bit run-down.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Tom
lines.text: No need to apologize. Safe travels, and I'll be in touch before four.

questions.q: What does Tom offer to do after Laura complains about the workaround?
options: Give Laura's company a refund
Have someone on his team send the invoices within the hour
Ask Laura's finance team to send the invoices manually
Call Laura's finance team about the invoices
questions.explain_zh: Tom 先提出 workaround（請 Laura 的團隊手動寄），Laura 不滿意後，他改說「someone on my team can send them for you within the hour」。

questions.q: Why does Laura say, "We're supposed to be saving time with your software"?
options: She thinks the workaround creates extra work for her team.
She wants Tom to send the invoices by Friday.
She has never used the billing page before.
She thinks the software is too expensive.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。她接著說「not adding work」：買軟體本來是為了省時間，要她們手動寄發票反而多出工作。

questions.q: When will Laura get a written report?
options: Before four o'clock
By Wednesday
By Friday
Next month
questions.explain_zh: Tom 說「you'll have a written report by Wednesday」。四點前是寄發票清單，Friday 是發票的截止日。

dictation: I've already escalated it to our engineers.
You don't have to wait for the fix, though.
We're supposed to be saving time with your software, not adding work.

shadowing: My finance team has to get those invoices out by Friday.
We're supposed to be saving time with your software.
You'd better make sure nothing falls through the cracks this time.
We're going to get to the bottom of it.

prompts.question: Your manager asks about a customer's bug. Give a one-sentence progress update with "supposed to" or "have to".
prompts.question_zh: 主管問你某個客戶的 bug 處理得怎樣。用 supposed to 或 have to 說一句進度（打字或小聲說都可以）。
prompts.sample: The fix was supposed to go out yesterday, but we have to run one more test first.

prompts.question: A teammate wants to promise an angry customer a refund. Warn them in one sentence.
prompts.question_zh: 同事想直接答應生氣的客戶退款。用一句話提醒他。
prompts.sample: You'd better check with your manager before you promise anything.

writing.task: A client's dashboard was down for three hours this morning. Write an email of 80-150 words to the client in three short parts: (1) apologize and say what happened, (2) explain what they can do for now and what you are doing, (3) say when they will hear from you next.
writing.task_zh: 客戶的儀表板今天早上當了三個小時。寫一封 80–150 個英文字的 email 給客戶，分三小段：(1) 道歉並說明發生什麼事；(2) 說明他們現在可以怎麼做、你們正在做什麼；(3) 說明下次什麼時候會再聯絡。
writing.sample:
Hi Dana,

I'm very sorry about this morning's outage. Your dashboard was down from 8 to 11 a.m., and the backup system that was supposed to take over didn't start. I know this issue first flared up in September, so I understand why you're frustrated.

For now, if the dashboard goes down again, your team doesn't have to track shipments by hand. There's a workaround: you can export shipment data every hour from the Reports page. Our engineers are working to get to the bottom of the problem today.

I'll send you an update by 5 p.m. today, and a full report by Friday.

Best regards,
Vincent
checklist_zh: 第一段：道歉＋發生什麼事（時間、影響）
第二段：現在可以用的 workaround＋你們正在做什麼
第三段：下次聯絡的明確時間
單數主詞（your team、the system）記得用 has／doesn't／was

translation.zh: 自從我們推出新版本以來，客訴已經減少了 30%。
translation.en: Since we launched the new version, complaints have dropped by 30%.
alt: Complaints have dropped by 30% since we launched the new version.
Since we launched the new version, complaints have gone down by 30%.
Since we released the new version, complaints have decreased by 30%.

translation.zh: 我到公司的時候，客戶已經寄了三封 email。
translation.en: By the time I got to the office, the client had already sent three emails.
alt: When I got to the office, the client had already sent three emails.
By the time I arrived at the office, the client had already sent three emails.

translation.zh: 她打電話來之前，她的團隊已經手動追蹤貨物一整個早上了。
translation.en: Before she called, her team had been tracking shipments by hand all morning.
alt: Her team had been tracking shipments by hand all morning before she called.
Before she called, her team had been tracking the shipments manually all morning.

translation.zh: 你最好先打電話給客戶，再寫 email。
translation.en: You'd better call the client before you write the email.
alt: You had better call the client before you write the email.
You'd better call the client first, before writing the email.
You'd better call the client first and then write the email.

translation.zh: 照規定，我們應該在兩小時內把問題往上呈報。
translation.en: Under our policy, we're supposed to escalate the problem within two hours.
alt: According to our policy, we're supposed to escalate the issue within two hours.
Under our policy, we are supposed to escalate the problem within two hours.

reading.title: When Saying Sorry Wins Customers Back
paragraphs: Every support team has a story about the customer who was furious on Monday and singing the team's praises by Friday. Researchers have a name for this: the service recovery paradox. The idea is simple. A customer whose problem is handled exceptionally well can end up more loyal than one who never had a problem at all.

The paradox has its limits, however. It tends to work only when the failure is minor, happens for the first time, and isn't obviously the company's fault. A second outage in two months is much harder to forgive, no matter how charming the apology may be. In other words, recovery is a safety net, not a strategy.

So what separates a recovery that wins customers back from one that drives them away? Speed matters, but tone matters more. Customers can tell within seconds whether they are being brushed off with a scripted apology or listened to by someone who genuinely owns the mistake. The best agents defuse anger by naming the problem before the customer has to, and by explaining what will happen next, even when the honest answer is "I don't know yet, but I'll call you at three."

Compensation, surprisingly, comes last. A generous refund offered too early can come across as an attempt to buy silence. Offered after the problem has been fixed, the same gesture reads as going the extra mile rather than paying the customer to go away.

Perhaps the most overlooked step happens weeks later. Following up once the dust has settled shows the customer that the apology wasn't just damage control. It is often in that quiet, unglamorous moment that a near-miss turns into a long-term relationship.

questions.q: According to the article, when is the service recovery paradox least likely to work?
options: When the problem is small and happens for the first time
When the same kind of failure happens again soon after
When the agent apologizes quickly
When the customer gets a refund after the fix
questions.explain_zh: 第 2 段：只有在問題小、第一次發生、又不明顯是公司的錯時才有效；「A second outage in two months is much harder to forgive」。

questions.q: Why might a refund offered too early backfire?
options: The customer may think the company is trying to keep them quiet.
The company may run out of money.
The customer may ask for an even bigger refund.
The refund may arrive after the problem is fixed.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。第 4 段說太早退款「can come across as an attempt to buy silence」，像是在花錢讓客戶閉嘴。

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about following up weeks later?
options: It is mainly a form of damage control.
Most companies already do it well.
It can quietly turn a bad experience into lasting trust.
It should replace the apology.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。最後一段說事後追蹤常被忽略，但往往就在那時「a near-miss turns into a long-term relationship」。

listening.title: How Did It Go with Northway?

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Ryan
lines.text: So, how did it go with Northway? I heard Dana was ready to cancel.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Mei
lines.text: She was. Honestly, the first ten minutes were rough. She just needed to vent, so I mostly kept quiet and took notes.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Ryan
lines.text: Smart. I'd have jumped straight to the refund.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Mei
lines.text: Yeah, I almost did, but, you know, if you lead with money, it sounds like you're trying to…

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Ryan
lines.text: Make them go away. Right.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Mei
lines.text: Exactly. So I owned it. I said, "We let you down, and it's the second time, which makes it worse."

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Ryan
lines.text: Wow, you actually said "second time"? Most people would dance around that.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Mei
lines.text: I figured she'd bring it up anyway. Better to defuse it before it turned into an argument.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Ryan
lines.text: Fair. And did you promise a date for the fix?

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Mei
lines.text: No, and that's the thing. I said I didn't know yet, but I'd call her at three with an update. And I did, right on the dot.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Ryan
lines.text: Huh. So no fancy script, just doing what you said you'd do.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Mei
lines.text: Pretty much. Turns out that's rarer than it should be.

questions.q: Why didn't Mei offer a refund at the start of the call?
options: Her manager had refused to approve one.
It might have sounded like she wanted the customer to go away.
Dana had already received a refund.
She forgot about it until Ryan mentioned it.
questions.explain_zh: Mei 說一開始就談錢「it sounds like you're trying to…」，Ryan 幫她接完「make them go away」。

questions.q: What does Ryan suggest when he says, "Most people would dance around that"?
options: Most people would avoid admitting it was the second failure.
Most people would apologize twice.
Most people would cancel the call.
Most people would offer a bigger refund.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。dance around 是「迴避、不直接講」。Ryan 驚訝 Mei 直接承認是「第二次」，表示多數人會避開這點。

questions.q: What did Mei promise Dana instead of a date for the fix?
options: A free month of service
A call at three with an update
A visit from the engineering lead
A written report by Friday
questions.explain_zh: Mei 說「I'd call her at three with an update. And I did, right on the dot.」

dictation: She just needed to vent, so I mostly kept quiet and took notes.
I figured she'd bring it up anyway.

glossary.definition: the idea that a customer whose problem is fixed very well can become more loyal than before
to treat someone's concern as unimportant and not deal with it properly
to accept that a mistake is yours and take responsibility for it
to make a tense or angry situation calmer
to make more effort than people expect
to avoid talking about something directly
